name: Rolling Forecasts
title: Rolling Forecasts
answer: Rolling forecasts are budgets and projections that are rebuilt at a fixed cadence, typically monthly or quarterly, so that the planning horizon always extends the same distance ahead. Instead of locking a twelve month plan at the start of the year and watching it age, a rolling forecast drops the period just ended and adds a new one at the far end. In finance and accounting teams the practice sits between the annual budget and the long range plan, and it is used for revenue, headcount, cash and cost lines that move often enough to make a static plan stale. The scope is usually the whole profit and loss statement at a summary level, with deeper detail only on the lines that drive decisions.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a planning layer that sits above the general ledger, most often a dedicated tool such as Anaplan, Pigment, Oracle EPM or a similar platform, fed by actuals extracted from the ERP. Spreadsheet models still carry a large share of rolling forecasts, particularly in mid sized companies, and they are the usual starting point before a team moves to a governed platform. The data pipeline matters more than the modelling engine: actuals, headcount files, pipeline data and currency rates all have to land on a schedule that matches the forecast cadence. Version control and a single source of truth for assumptions are what separate a workable rolling process from a monthly scramble.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A rolling forecast is built by taking the latest actuals, comparing them with the prior forecast, and then re forecasting the remaining periods with updated drivers. Driver based models, where revenue is a function of volume and price or headcount is a function of hiring plans, hold up better than line by line extrapolation because the assumptions stay visible. Many teams now blend statistical forecasts from historical data with judgemental overlays from business owners, and machine learning is used mainly on high volume, repeatable lines such as transaction revenue or support costs. The cadence is the discipline: a short, consistent cycle with clear ownership beats a detailed model that is rebuilt twice a year.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because a rolling forecast is refreshed constantly, the audit trail and the version history carry more weight than they do for an annual budget. Teams need to record which assumptions changed, who approved the change, and how the new forecast compares with the prior one, so that the numbers can be explained to a board or an auditor months later. Access controls matter where sensitive items such as compensation or restructuring sit in the same model as published figures. Where forecasts feed external reporting or covenant calculations, the provenance of the underlying data and the reconciliation back to the ledger become part of the control environment rather than an afterthought.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward shorter cycles and more continuous re forecasting, with actuals flowing in automatically and the forecast updating as a matter of routine rather than as a monthly event. Scenario planning is being folded into the same model, so a team can hold a base case, an upside and a downside without maintaining three separate files. Machine learning is likely to take over more of the high volume lines, leaving finance to own the judgemental drivers and the narrative. The constraint is rarely the software, it is the willingness of the business to commit to a cadence and to keep the assumptions honest.
